query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Coupling high‐resolution DSC and high‐temperature dilatometry with CALPHAD-based configurational entropy corrections will accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, as-cast high-entropy alloys (e.g., equiatomic alloys with disordered fcc or bcc lattices) before melting.
generation.intervention: Apply precise differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure the sharp cp increase at the solidus and latent heat of fusion, combined with high-temperature dilatometry to monitor volume changes, and use CALPHAD modeling that incorporates configurational entropy to interpret and extend the experimental data.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted under inert or vacuum atmosphere to avoid oxidation, using controlled heating rates that allow for clear resolution of thermal transitions (from cryogenic temperatures up through and beyond the melting transition).
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy inherent to HEAs mediates a homogenized Gibbs free-energy landscape, enabling the use of mixing models and adjusted CALPHAD parameters to relate experimental heat capacity and expansion data to fusion properties.
generation.mechanism: The entropic stabilization of the HEA phases modifies the relative contributions of enthalpy and entropy upon melting. By measuring the heat capacity evolution (including the Debye T^3 behavior at low T and the Dulong–Petit limit at room temperature) and the latent heat jump at T_m, one can derive ΔH_f and ΔS_f, while concurrent dilatometry yields the melting volume change. Incorporation of CALPHAD with configurational entropy corrections then allows these experimental observables to be extrapolated and generalized across different alloy compositions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated experimental/modeling approach is expected to yield melting temperature, ΔH_f, ΔS_f, and ΔV_m values that agree with CALPHAD predictions and literature data within an error margin of approximately 5–10% for HEAs with a single-phase high-symmetry structure. The method should efficiently resolve key thermodynamic properties despite the chemical complexity and sluggish diffusion in HEAs.
generation.baseline: Standard DSC and dilatometry measurements without CALPHAD integration typically yield qualitative trends; the integrated method is predicted to provide quantitative improvements in accuracy and efficiency.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable primarily to entropy-stabilized, single-phase HEAs. Its performance may be limited in multi-phase or strongly segregated alloys where the individual phase contributions cannot be deconvoluted with the same confidence.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports the use of DSC, dilatometry, and CALPHAD in similar contexts, uncertainties remain regarding the absolute quantification in HEAs with complex phase equilibria or for alloys that deviate significantly from ideal mixing behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Select several HEA compositions that are known or suspected to form multi-phase microstructures. Perform DSC measurement to capture cp and latent heat transitions and simultaneous high-temperature dilatometry to record volume change. Apply the CALPHAD-based adjustment to predict thermodynamic properties and compare these with the independently measured values. A secondary set of experiments on well-established single-phase HEAs should also be carried out as controls.
measurements: DSC trace showing a distinct jump in cp at the solidus line and associated latent heat ΔH_f
Dilatometry curve indicating the volume jump ΔV_m at the melting transition
Calculated ΔS_f from both DSC data and integrated CALPHAD entropy contributions
Comparison of predicted thermodynamic properties with literature or benchmark CALPHAD results
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally determined melting temperature, ΔH_f, ΔS_f, or ΔV_m deviate by more than 10% from the CALPHAD-adjusted predictions in single-phase HEAs, or if the method fails to produce consistent results across a representative range of HEA compositions, then the proposed integrated approach is falsified.

The Calphad approach is used widely in the high entropy alloys and ceramics field [,,]. Senkov et al. demonstrated [] that for high entropy alloys, Calphad computations of type and number of phases agreed well with experimental results only when more than half of binary systems were fully assessed; however, even when there are enough data on binary and ternary systems, Calphad predictions of transformation temperatures, phase compositions and fractions are challenging. Compared with metals, the databases for oxides are much more limited, especially for the temperature range addressed in this study. Nevertheless, it is instructive to compare our experimental results with Calphad predictions.

For temperatures close to room temperature (RT) the heat capacity is close to 3R if there is no change in magnetic behavior and no phase transformation. This is known as the Dulong-Petit law, which states that every solid that consists of N atoms has 3N modes of vibration (corresponding to the freedom of motion in three dimensions). Energetic considerations using the equipartition theorem lead to cp = 3·R for sufficiently high temperatures (RT).
